Fake Injectors

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Exposing South Africa’s underground injector economy

Unique Selling Point:
Exploring South Africa’s underground world of unlicensed Botox and filler injectors, where air hostesses and strippers perform medical procedures - illegally and with unauthorised products.

Summary:
The aesthetics boom isn’t just for the rich - it’s become a cultural movement. But beneath the filters, something darker brews.

Picture this.
You’re scrolling through social media and come across an advert for injectables - fillers and Botox - offered by an ‘aesthetic doctor’ in Cape Town for a fraction of the usual costs.
According to her profile - which boasts thousands of followers and pictures of dozens of ‘before’ and ‘after’ pictures of clients,
‘Dr’ Vanessa Sobol is a Russian cosmetologist with over 10 years of experience helping clients achieve their beauty goals.
She also works as a stripper at Mavericks nightclub in downtown Cape Town - while moonlighting as a medical professional who offers training in lip fillers and other dermal filler treatments - with certification - for R20 000.
In South Africa, only a doctor or dentist registered with the Health Professions Council of South Africa (HPCSA) can legally inject dermal fillers and Botox, and its illegal for anyone else to perform these treatments - given the potential risks.
But Sobol is just one of a number of untrained injectors that have been flooding social media platforms like Instagram of late, offering aesthetic procedures at often too-good-to-be-true or exorbitant prices.
‘Bare Aesthetics’ is run by a flight attendant for FlySafair, Karolinah Nunes, and offers mobile filler and Botox treatments, as well as ‘Botox parties’.
She also sells black market Ozempic at a third of the actual price. Ozempic can only be prescribed by a medical doctor in South Africa.

While these illegal injectors continue to perform these procedures without authorisation, another concern is of the safety and efficacy of the products being used - many of which are cheap, counterfeit, non-medical grade and dangerous products purchased from China, Korea and the black market.
The dealing in unregulated scheduled medical substances is both illegal and an extreme safety risk to patients.
Experts say that these counterfeits most commonly lead to bizarre infections and abcessess and bacteremias, also due to unsterile manufacturing techniques.
Necrosis of tissue is also a common cause, and these illegal products can also lead to severe allergic reactions, anaphylaxis, and even death.
Long term effects can include nodule formations, disfigurement, and severe deformities.

Registered aesthetic and cosmetic doctors who are members of the Aesthetic and Anti-Aging Medicine Society of South Africa (AAAMSSA) say the situation is becoming worse on a daily basis, and even though they’re constantly reporting unlicensed injectors and fake doctors to the HPCSA and SAHPRA, nothing is seemingly being done to hold these charlatans to account.
Fraudsters impersonating healthcare professionals training the lay person is also hugely concerning, given that anyone can now be able to inject filler into another person’s face.
They say that counterfeit doses and unlicensed providers are harming patients, and that procedures are being performed in makeshift medical offices - including Airbnb’s, and that these criminals’ are contributing to
the burgeoning black market with unlicensed and counterfeit botox and fillers from South Korea and China.
It’s estimated that in South Africa, unlicensed injections outnumber legitimate licensed practitioners three to one - with one-quarter of procedures being done in someone’s home/makeshift medical setting, rather than at an accredited clinic.

* This story will investigate and expose serious flaws in the South African beauty and aesthetics industry - that are endangering lives, and leaving people at risk of being scarred for life.

* It will also examine the true cost of beauty in South Africa, and what needs to be done to ensure that the safety of patients is maintained in aesthetic medicine - when the market is being flooded by counterfeit medical professionals and counterfeit goods?

Press Release:


The Beauty Underground
In the flourishing world of unlicensed cosmetics, air hostesses and exotic dancers are performing illegal medical procedures with unauthorised products – at a fraction of the usual cost. But what sounds too good to be true usually is. Counterfeit, non-medical grade products can cause infection, allergic reactions and long-term complications. As unregistered, untrained injectors flood social media to advertise their services, thousands of customers are signing up. Can anything be done to hold them to account?
Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Lourensa Eckard

Script:


FAKE INJECTORS: FINAL DRAFT

(Lourensa): “Jet-set lives. Flawless feeds. Designer everything…”

(Lourensa): “On social media, beauty sells.”

(Lourensa): “But beneath the filters and followers, something darker is being injected.”

(Tara): “I put my trust in someone who misrepresented themselves... I didn’t consent to this level of danger… it honestly does feel like assault.”

(Fawzia): “What we’re now seeing is a field completely saturated with these criminals, impersonating healthcare practitioners.”

(Lourensa): “It’s a world with alleged links to organised crime.... leading to a climate of silence and fear…”

(Lourensa): “In the mirror, everything seems flawless. But reflections can lie. And behind the glow, a dangerous underworld is hiding… in plain sight.”

(Lourensa): “Botox and dermal fillers are the holy grail of modern beauty treatments. They erase wrinkles, plump lips, sculpt cheekbones… all in minutes, with a simple injection.”

(Lourensa): “But don’t be fooled; these aren’t cosmetics. They’re regulated medical-grade injectables - meant for licensed medical professionals.”

(Lourensa): “And in the wrong hands - they can disfigure

(Lourensa): “Inside this medical centre behind me, a woman - known simply as ‘Dr Vanessa’ - runs one of Cape Town’s busiest underground aesthetic clinics.
She’s not a licensed doctor, but influencers swear by her needle.”

(Lourensa): “*Anna – not her real name – thought she was in safe hands.”

(Anna): “I couldn’t drive because I didn’t feel well. And then I went to the bathroom, and that was the time when I saw the one side of my face was a bit skew, and my lips.

(Lourensa): “So when you went back a few weeks later, it was Dr Vanessa that dissolved what was injected initially and redid the fillers, is that correct?”
(Anna): ‘That’s correct, yes.’
(Lourensa): “What did she tell you?”
(Anna): ‘She didn’t tell me anything. She just told Dr Des that she took the wrong needle and placed it too deep, something like that. And that was the time when she took a thick needle to dissolve it, and redo it.’
(Lourensa): “She dissolved it and did the filler during the same session?”
(Anna): ‘The same time, ya.’
(Lourensa): “Was it painful?”
(Anna): ‘It was, it was very painful.”

(Lourensa): “Four months after the injections, *Anna’s lips were full of hard nodules and deep bruises. Renowned aesthetic doctor Hildegardt Raubenheimer stepped in.”

(Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “The dangers with not having a medical professional inject a face is that they have no clue about the anatomy of the face, they have no clue of the physiology; they have no clue about how products respond within the tissue, and also they don’t know to recognise and how to manage complications.”
(Lourensa): “Raubenheimer sees the results of beauty therapists playing doctor all too often.”
(Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “We are performing medical procedures. We have the knowledge, we have the skill that take years to hone… We are not doing beauty procedures. We are injecting people’s faces - and that has to be regulated, because any medical procedure can have adverse events.”
(Lourensa): “In untrained hands, filler can block arteries, kill skin, trigger strokes - even cause blindness or paralysis.”
(Dr Vanessa): “Here we can add a little bit filler here, but after Botox.”

(Lourensa): “We went undercover to see how Dr Vanessa works.”

(Lourensa): “She calls herself a doctor - but the Health Professions Council, the body that licenses real medical professionals, says otherwise. We’ve established that she’s done a beauty course abroad… and has confirmed ties to a gentleman’s club in downtown Cape Town.”
(H): “Where did you learn all these things?”
(Dr Vanessa): “I studied in Russia…”
(H): “You just know too much…”
(Dr Vanessa): “I went to school, you know, the beauty medical industry but its in my peril - very big competition. Here no competition.” (laughs)

(Lourensa):
“She’s even teaching her craft, offering six-hour courses to anyone with the cash to spare.”

(Dr Vanessa): “Yes, so if they want real technique, we can come to me, I teach. For lips: five technique of augmentation, one day, R15 000…”
(H): 15?
(Dr Vanessa): “But I will not give for official document from university, you know.”

(Tara): “Now that I know I was at medical risk for something that was just meant to enhance my beauty, I kind of feel, just like, shocked and betrayed.”

(Lourensa): “This woman, we’ll call *Tara, is another of Dr Vanessa’s unfortunate clients, and only narrowly escaped permanent damage.”

(Tara): “The filler was injected into a blood vessel, which means (the) blood couldn’t flow in my lips, which if it was left untreated it could have caused tissue death in my lip.”

(Lourensa): “Left any longer, part of her face could’ve died. Aesthetic doctor and licensed trainer, Fawzia Salie stepped in - dissolving the filler and saving Tara’s lips.”

(Dr Fawzia Salie) ‘Psychologically it takes a toll on these patients. Financially too. They feel scammed.’’

(Lourensa): “We’ve noticed through our investigations that a lot of these illegal injectors are foreigners?”
(Dr Fawzia Salie): “What we’re seeing is an influx of these so-called cosmetologists, beauticians… we’re even seeing exotic dancers, so our industry is rife with unregulated criminals.”

(Lourensa): “Is there a sense of fear - uhm, for people that are perhaps afraid to speak out?”
(Dr Fawzia Salie): “Absolutely. I think there’s a large sense of shame in having to had to have gone to these practitioners - if I may call them such - in the first place.
But there is a second darker element to this. I think these patients fear for their lives, I think they’re worried; I think they’re afraid of being victimised, or physically hurt.”
(Lourensa): “Is this because of the kind of people that are involved in this industry?”
(Dr Fawzia Salie): “I think yes… I think it’s all one big dark sort of underworld, brewing.”

(Lourensa): “But alleged underworld ties aren’t the only way to access and administer unlicensed injectables. Our investigation revealed someone not involved in the criminal underworld but who simply went from client to practitioner.”

(Lourensa): “Carolina Nunes. I understand that she was one of your patients?”
(Dr Fawzia Salie): “Carolina first saw me as a patient… but Carolina had started to message me asking me about whether there was a way she could safely inject in South Africa. I had proceeded to tell her that in South Africa we’re governed by a strict set of laws - that you’ve got to be a medical doctor or a registered dentist in order to practice aesthetic medicine.”
(Lourensa): “So that was made clear to her?”
(Dr Fawzia Salie): “It was made clear, by me to her - yes.”

(Lourensa): “Carolina Nunes is a flight attendant…”

(Carolina Nunes): “So my product that I get is a lot cheaper, but all the Russians use it…”
(Lourensa): “While we can’t say she’s caused direct harm - others have.”
(Lourensa): “And that’s why Carolina Nunes matters. She’s part of a growing black market.”
(Carolina Nunes): “I charge R1600 for 0.5mls, and R2400 for a mil of filler.”

(Lourensa): “So we posed as clients.”
(Carolina Nunes): “I only charge like R55 a unit for Botox so it’s really affordable… but I like to keep my prices low for people who aren’t able to spend like R5000 every time they want to top up a few lines on their face.”

(Lourensa): “R55 for a unit for Botox sounds like a steal, but there’s a reason it’s cheap. Fillers? Same story. The real stuff is medical-grade, clinically-tested, and costs double… because your face isn’t economy class.”
(Lourensa): “Carolina Nunes is an air hostess, she’s trained to serve at 35 000 feet - not to handle syringes. She has no licence, she’s not a medical doctor; she has no business injecting anything into anyone. It’s a dangerous game of cosmetic roulette, and we’re about to bring her in… for a hard landing.”
(Lourensa): “Hi, Carolina, hi.”
(Carolina Nunes): “Yes…”
(Lourensa): “We’re from Carte Blanche. We just want to ask you a few questions about what you’re doing here. Is that okay?”
(Carolina Nunes): “Uhm, no, sorry…”
(Lourensa): “Are you a trained medical professional?”
(Carolina Nunes): “No, I do microneedling and dermaplaning.”
(Lourensa): “Well we’ve spoken to people who you’ve injected, and who you’ve advertised your services to…”
(Carolina Nunes): “Okay, well you’re not allowed to be on my property…”
(Lourensa): “Do you know what you’re doing is illegal?”
(Carolina Nunes): “Sorry love, I don’t do any of that stuff, so this is all microneedling and dermaplaning…”
(Lourensa): “What are you saying to the people? Do your clients know that you’re not trained?”
(Carolina Nunes): “Sorry, you’re not allowed on my property…”
(Lourensa): “Where do you get your products, Carolina?”
(Door shuts) We just wanted to ask you a few questions. Carolina?”

(Lourensa): “Her reaction suggested that Carolina was familiar with the law. Having denied injecting people, we gave her another chance to explain.”

(Carolina Nunes): “You are making accusations. I'm absolutely … I think you actually have the wrong person…”
(Lourensa): “Well, we’d love your response to those accusations; we want to give you the opportunity to state your side…”
(Carolina Nunes): “Well I have no idea what you’re talking about.”
(Carolina Nunes): ‘You are literally not allowed anywhere near my property or anywhere near me, because I will call my lawyer and I will call the police.’
(Lourensa:) “Carolina, do your clients know that you have no medical training?”
(Lourensa): “She hung up.”

—————————-
(Lourensa): “In South Africa, only medical doctors and dentists are allowed to procure and administer regulated aesthetic products - like Botox and fillers. But our investigation has revealed that some of these illegal injectors are bringing in unregulated products from China, Russia, and Korea. We were even able to buy some off Temu.”
(Lourensa): “We asked Dr Raubenheimer for her thoughts on what we’d bought for just R200 online.”

(Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): Looks like it’s valid…”
(Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “Looks like a filler, but we have no idea what’s inside here.”
(Lourensa): “But how easy is that? You put on a needle and you’re able to inject someone with it, or inject yourself.”
(Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “Yeah, the petrol guy can do it.”
(Lourensa): “How dangerous is that?”
(Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “Very dangerous.”

(Lourensa): “If nothing changes, what do you think would be the worst case scenario in South Africa?”
(Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “We will definitely see an increase of more serious complications; tissue death, necrosis, possible blindness, and even death.”

(Lourensa): “Many countries jail fake injectors. Here, they slip through the cracks - exotic dancers by night, doctors by day. And, fearing victimisation, their clients keep their lips sealed.”

(Lourensa): “We tried contacting Dr Vanessa but she never responded, just vanished online - and from her treatment rooms. Carolina’s employers told us her job is under review. Her lawyers said she’s chosen to reserve her right of reply. As for the clients, many become the victims of unregulated beauty, burdened by the cost of repairing botched procedures and, in some cases, permanently scarred.

(Anna): “It is traumatising, because elke vrou wil beautiful lyk… I want to look international, and we all want to look international, but ons wil nie ‘botched’ lyk nie.”

(Lourensa) “What would you say to someone considering going to one of these social media injectors?
(Dr Fawzia Salie) “Ask yourself: ‘Would you go to the lady who does your regular waxing, to operate on your heart?’’
(Lourensa) “It’s that serious?”
(Dr Fawzia Salie) ‘It’s serious.’

But what sounds too good to be true usually is. Counterfeit, non-medical grade products can cause infection, allergic reactions and long-term complications. As unregistered, untrained injectors flood social media to advertise their services, thousands of customers are signing up. Can anything be done to hold them to account? Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Lourensa Eckard Script: FAKE INJECTORS: FINAL DRAFT (Lourensa): “Jet-set lives. Flawless feeds. Designer everything…” (Lourensa): “On social media, beauty sells.” (Lourensa): “But beneath the filters and followers, something darker is being injected.” (Tara): “I put my trust in someone who misrepresented themselves... I didn’t consent to this level of danger… it honestly does feel like assault.” (Fawzia): “What we’re now seeing is a field completely saturated with these criminals, impersonating healthcare practitioners.” (Lourensa): “It’s a world with alleged links to organised crime.... leading to a climate of silence and fear…” (Lourensa): “In the mirror, everything seems flawless. But reflections can lie. And behind the glow, a dangerous underworld is hiding… in plain sight.” (Lourensa): “Botox and dermal fillers are the holy grail of modern beauty treatments. They erase wrinkles, plump lips, sculpt cheekbones… all in minutes, with a simple injection.” (Lourensa): “But don’t be fooled; these aren’t cosmetics. They’re regulated medical-grade injectables - meant for licensed medical professionals.” (Lourensa): “And in the wrong hands - they can disfigure (Lourensa): “Inside this medical centre behind me, a woman - known simply as ‘Dr Vanessa’ - runs one of Cape Town’s busiest underground aesthetic clinics. She’s not a licensed doctor, but influencers swear by her needle.” (Lourensa): “*Anna – not her real name – thought she was in safe hands.” (Anna): “I couldn’t drive because I didn’t feel well. And then I went to the bathroom, and that was the time when I saw the one side of my face was a bit skew, and my lips. (Lourensa): “So when you went back a few weeks later, it was Dr Vanessa that dissolved what was injected initially and redid the fillers, is that correct?” (Anna): ‘That’s correct, yes.’ (Lourensa): “What did she tell you?” (Anna): ‘She didn’t tell me anything. She just told Dr Des that she took the wrong needle and placed it too deep, something like that. And that was the time when she took a thick needle to dissolve it, and redo it.’ (Lourensa): “She dissolved it and did the filler during the same session?” (Anna): ‘The same time, ya.’ (Lourensa): “Was it painful?” (Anna): ‘It was, it was very painful.” (Lourensa): “Four months after the injections, *Anna’s lips were full of hard nodules and deep bruises. Renowned aesthetic doctor Hildegardt Raubenheimer stepped in.” (Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “The dangers with not having a medical professional inject a face is that they have no clue about the anatomy of the face, they have no clue of the physiology; they have no clue about how products respond within the tissue, and also they don’t know to recognise and how to manage complications.” (Lourensa): “Raubenheimer sees the results of beauty therapists playing doctor all too often.” (Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “We are performing medical procedures. We have the knowledge, we have the skill that take years to hone… We are not doing beauty procedures. We are injecting people’s faces - and that has to be regulated, because any medical procedure can have adverse events.” (Lourensa): “In untrained hands, filler can block arteries, kill skin, trigger strokes - even cause blindness or paralysis.” (Dr Vanessa): “Here we can add a little bit filler here, but after Botox.” (Lourensa): “We went undercover to see how Dr Vanessa works.” (Lourensa): “She calls herself a doctor - but the Health Professions Council, the body that licenses real medical professionals, says otherwise. We’ve established that she’s done a beauty course abroad… and has confirmed ties to a gentleman’s club in downtown Cape Town.” (H): “Where did you learn all these things?” (Dr Vanessa): “I studied in Russia…” (H): “You just know too much…” (Dr Vanessa): “I went to school, you know, the beauty medical industry but its in my peril - very big competition. Here no competition.” (laughs) (Lourensa): “She’s even teaching her craft, offering six-hour courses to anyone with the cash to spare.” (Dr Vanessa): “Yes, so if they want real technique, we can come to me, I teach. For lips: five technique of augmentation, one day, R15 000…” (H): 15? (Dr Vanessa): “But I will not give for official document from university, you know.” (Tara): “Now that I know I was at medical risk for something that was just meant to enhance my beauty, I kind of feel, just like, shocked and betrayed.” (Lourensa): “This woman, we’ll call *Tara, is another of Dr Vanessa’s unfortunate clients, and only narrowly escaped permanent damage.” (Tara): “The filler was injected into a blood vessel, which means (the) blood couldn’t flow in my lips, which if it was left untreated it could have caused tissue death in my lip.” (Lourensa): “Left any longer, part of her face could’ve died. Aesthetic doctor and licensed trainer, Fawzia Salie stepped in - dissolving the filler and saving Tara’s lips.” (Dr Fawzia Salie) ‘Psychologically it takes a toll on these patients. Financially too. They feel scammed.’’ (Lourensa): “We’ve noticed through our investigations that a lot of these illegal injectors are foreigners?” (Dr Fawzia Salie): “What we’re seeing is an influx of these so-called cosmetologists, beauticians… we’re even seeing exotic dancers, so our industry is rife with unregulated criminals.” (Lourensa): “Is there a sense of fear - uhm, for people that are perhaps afraid to speak out?” (Dr Fawzia Salie): “Absolutely. I think there’s a large sense of shame in having to had to have gone to these practitioners - if I may call them such - in the first place. But there is a second darker element to this. I think these patients fear for their lives, I think they’re worried; I think they’re afraid of being victimised, or physically hurt.” (Lourensa): “Is this because of the kind of people that are involved in this industry?” (Dr Fawzia Salie): “I think yes… I think it’s all one big dark sort of underworld, brewing.” (Lourensa): “But alleged underworld ties aren’t the only way to access and administer unlicensed injectables. Our investigation revealed someone not involved in the criminal underworld but who simply went from client to practitioner.” (Lourensa): “Carolina Nunes. I understand that she was one of your patients?” (Dr Fawzia Salie): “Carolina first saw me as a patient… but Carolina had started to message me asking me about whether there was a way she could safely inject in South Africa. I had proceeded to tell her that in South Africa we’re governed by a strict set of laws - that you’ve got to be a medical doctor or a registered dentist in order to practice aesthetic medicine.” (Lourensa): “So that was made clear to her?” (Dr Fawzia Salie): “It was made clear, by me to her - yes.” (Lourensa): “Carolina Nunes is a flight attendant…” (Carolina Nunes): “So my product that I get is a lot cheaper, but all the Russians use it…” (Lourensa): “While we can’t say she’s caused direct harm - others have.” (Lourensa): “And that’s why Carolina Nunes matters. She’s part of a growing black market.” (Carolina Nunes): “I charge R1600 for 0.5mls, and R2400 for a mil of filler.” (Lourensa): “So we posed as clients.” (Carolina Nunes): “I only charge like R55 a unit for Botox so it’s really affordable… but I like to keep my prices low for people who aren’t able to spend like R5000 every time they want to top up a few lines on their face.” (Lourensa): “R55 for a unit for Botox sounds like a steal, but there’s a reason it’s cheap. Fillers? Same story. The real stuff is medical-grade, clinically-tested, and costs double… because your face isn’t economy class.” (Lourensa): “Carolina Nunes is an air hostess, she’s trained to serve at 35 000 feet - not to handle syringes. She has no licence, she’s not a medical doctor; she has no business injecting anything into anyone. It’s a dangerous game of cosmetic roulette, and we’re about to bring her in… for a hard landing.” (Lourensa): “Hi, Carolina, hi.” (Carolina Nunes): “Yes…” (Lourensa): “We’re from Carte Blanche. We just want to ask you a few questions about what you’re doing here. Is that okay?” (Carolina Nunes): “Uhm, no, sorry…” (Lourensa): “Are you a trained medical professional?” (Carolina Nunes): “No, I do microneedling and dermaplaning.” (Lourensa): “Well we’ve spoken to people who you’ve injected, and who you’ve advertised your services to…” (Carolina Nunes): “Okay, well you’re not allowed to be on my property…” (Lourensa): “Do you know what you’re doing is illegal?” (Carolina Nunes): “Sorry love, I don’t do any of that stuff, so this is all microneedling and dermaplaning…” (Lourensa): “What are you saying to the people? Do your clients know that you’re not trained?” (Carolina Nunes): “Sorry, you’re not allowed on my property…” (Lourensa): “Where do you get your products, Carolina?” (Door shuts) We just wanted to ask you a few questions. Carolina?” (Lourensa): “Her reaction suggested that Carolina was familiar with the law. Having denied injecting people, we gave her another chance to explain.” (Carolina Nunes): “You are making accusations. I'm absolutely … I think you actually have the wrong person…” (Lourensa): “Well, we’d love your response to those accusations; we want to give you the opportunity to state your side…” (Carolina Nunes): “Well I have no idea what you’re talking about.” (Carolina Nunes): ‘You are literally not allowed anywhere near my property or anywhere near me, because I will call my lawyer and I will call the police.’ (Lourensa:) “Carolina, do your clients know that you have no medical training?” (Lourensa): “She hung up.” —————————- (Lourensa): “In South Africa, only medical doctors and dentists are allowed to procure and administer regulated aesthetic products - like Botox and fillers. But our investigation has revealed that some of these illegal injectors are bringing in unregulated products from China, Russia, and Korea. We were even able to buy some off Temu.” (Lourensa): “We asked Dr Raubenheimer for her thoughts on what we’d bought for just R200 online.” (Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): Looks like it’s valid…” (Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “Looks like a filler, but we have no idea what’s inside here.” (Lourensa): “But how easy is that? You put on a needle and you’re able to inject someone with it, or inject yourself.” (Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “Yeah, the petrol guy can do it.” (Lourensa): “How dangerous is that?” (Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “Very dangerous.” (Lourensa): “If nothing changes, what do you think would be the worst case scenario in South Africa?” (Dr Hildegardt Raubenheimer): “We will definitely see an increase of more serious complications; tissue death, necrosis, possible blindness, and even death.” (Lourensa): “Many countries jail fake injectors. Here, they slip through the cracks - exotic dancers by night, doctors by day. And, fearing victimisation, their clients keep their lips sealed.” (Lourensa): “We tried contacting Dr Vanessa but she never responded, just vanished online - and from her treatment rooms. Carolina’s employers told us her job is under review. Her lawyers said she’s chosen to reserve her right of reply. As for the clients, many become the victims of unregulated beauty, burdened by the cost of repairing botched procedures and, in some cases, permanently scarred. (Anna): “It is traumatising, because elke vrou wil beautiful lyk… I want to look international, and we all want to look international, but ons wil nie ‘botched’ lyk nie.” (Lourensa) “What would you say to someone considering going to one of these social media injectors? (Dr Fawzia Salie) “Ask yourself: ‘Would you go to the lady who does your regular waxing, to operate on your heart?’’ (Lourensa) “It’s that serious?” (Dr Fawzia Salie) ‘It’s serious.’ —————————

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Exposing South Africa’s underground injector economy
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Exploring South Africa’s underground world of unlicensed Botox and filler injectors, where air hostesses and strippers perform medical procedures - illegally and with unauthorised products.
metadata.Summary: The aesthetics boom isn’t just for the rich - it’s become a cultural movement. But beneath the filters, something darker brews. Picture this. You’re scrolling through social media and come across an advert for injectables - fillers and Botox - offered by an ‘aesthetic doctor’ in Cape Town for a fraction of the usual costs. According to her profile - which boasts thousands of followers and pictures of dozens of ‘before’ and ‘after’ pictures of clients, ‘Dr’ Vanessa Sobol is a Russian cosmetologist with over 10 years of experience helping clients achieve their beauty goals. She also works as a stripper at Mavericks nightclub in downtown Cape Town - while moonlighting as a medical professional who offers training in lip fillers and other dermal filler treatments - with certification - for R20 000. In South Africa, only a doctor or dentist registered with the Health Professions Council of South Africa (HPCSA) can legally inject dermal fillers and Botox, and its illegal for anyone else to perform these treatments - given the potential risks. But Sobol is just one of a number of untrained injectors that have been flooding social media platforms like Instagram of late, offering aesthetic procedures at often too-good-to-be-true or exorbitant prices. ‘Bare Aesthetics’ is run by a flight attendant for FlySafair, Karolinah Nunes, and offers mobile filler and Botox treatments, as well as ‘Botox parties’. She also sells black market Ozempic at a third of the actual price. Ozempic can only be prescribed by a medical doctor in South Africa. While these illegal injectors continue to perform these procedures without authorisation, another concern is of the safety and efficacy of the products being used - many of which are cheap, counterfeit, non-medical grade and dangerous products purchased from China, Korea and the black market. The dealing in unregulated scheduled medical substances is both illegal and an extreme safety risk to patients. Experts say that these counterfeits most commonly lead to bizarre infections and abcessess and bacteremias, also due to unsterile manufacturing techniques. Necrosis of tissue is also a common cause, and these illegal products can also lead to severe allergic reactions, anaphylaxis, and even death. Long term effects can include nodule formations, disfigurement, and severe deformities. Registered aesthetic and cosmetic doctors who are members of the Aesthetic and Anti-Aging Medicine Society of South Africa (AAAMSSA) say the situation is becoming worse on a daily basis, and even though they’re constantly reporting unlicensed injectors and fake doctors to the HPCSA and SAHPRA, nothing is seemingly being done to hold these charlatans to account. Fraudsters impersonating healthcare professionals training the lay person is also hugely concerning, given that anyone can now be able to inject filler into another person’s face. They say that counterfeit doses and unlicensed providers are harming patients, and that procedures are being performed in makeshift medical offices - including Airbnb’s, and that these criminals’ are contributing to the burgeoning black market with unlicensed and counterfeit botox and fillers from South Korea and China. It’s estimated that in South Africa, unlicensed injections outnumber legitimate licensed practitioners three to one - with one-quarter of procedures being done in someone’s home/makeshift medical setting, rather than at an accredited clinic. * This story will investigate and expose serious flaws in the South African beauty and aesthetics industry - that are endangering lives, and leaving people at risk of being scarred for life. * It will also examine the true cost of beauty in South Africa, and what needs to be done to ensure that the safety of patients is maintained in aesthetic medicine - when the market is being flooded by counterfeit medical professionals and counterfeit goods?
